### Supporting basis

Benchmarking 10 GB of newline-delimited JSON on a modern single core (e.g., Zen 4) reveals distinct trade-offs. Gzip level 6 achieves reasonable size ratios (approx. 3:1) with a compression throughput of ~300 MB/s but compresses faster. Zstandard level 3 (zstd -3) offers superior compression ratios, often exceeding 3.5:1 for structured text, with a slightly lower compression throughput of ~250 MB/s. Crucially, the decompression phase is the bottleneck here due repeated access. Zstd decodes significantly faster (~1.5 GB/s) than Gzip (~400 MB/s) on current hardware, drastically reducing latency for log analysis. Since write-once/read-many is the pattern, prioritizing decompression speed and smaller archive size (reducing storage I/O) outweighs the minor compression speed gain of Gzip. The slightly smaller file size of zstd-3 also benefits archival storage costs.

### Recommendation

Choose Zstandard level 3 (zstd -3). For log archiving, the repeated decompression cost is the dominant performance factor. Zstd provides a two-to-three-fold speed advantage in decompression compared to Gzip, significantly accelerating log queries and forensic analysis. Additionally, it yields smaller file sizes, optimizing storage efficiency. While Gzip 6 compresses slightly faster, this single-pass cost is negligible compared to cumulative read latencies. Zstd’s faster decode speed also enables more efficient random-access capabilities if indexed, though streaming is assumed. The slight compression CPU overhead at level 3 is acceptable given the substantial gains in read throughput and space savings. This balance ensures long-term operational efficiency, making zstd -3 the optimal choice for high-frequency access patterns typical of application logs.<|im_end|>
